summary: Psalm 122 begins with gladness at being invited to Yahweh’s house and then places the speaker inside Jerusalem’s gates. The poem looks at Jerusalem as a gathered city for Israel’s tribes, a place of thanksgiving and judgment, and ends by asking for peace and seeking the city’s good for the sake of people and Yahweh’s house.
whyItMatters: This psalm belongs to Book V’s pilgrimage material, where worship, Jerusalem, and communal prayer come into focus. It shows love for the city not as scenery but as concern for worship, justice, companions, and peace.

context.author: The heading says, “A Song of Ascents. By David.” In Psalms, such headings are ancient parts of the transmitted collection, but readers differ on whether “By David” always means authorship, association, dedication, or belonging to a Davidic collection.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, especially readers or singers who understand Jerusalem and Yahweh’s house as central to common worship.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 122 is uncertain.
context.setting: A pilgrimage voice arrives at Jerusalem, names its gates, tribes, thrones, walls, palaces, companions, and the house of Yahweh.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry within the Songs of Ascents, a group of psalms associated in the headings with going up.

outline.heading: Glad invitation
outline.note: The speaker remembers joy when others said to go to Yahweh’s house.

outline.heading: Arrival in Jerusalem
outline.note: The pilgrims’ feet are now inside Jerusalem’s gates.

outline.heading: The gathered city
outline.note: Jerusalem is pictured as a compact city where Yah’s tribes go up to give thanks to Yahweh’s name.

outline.heading: Judgment and David’s house
outline.note: The city is also associated with thrones for judgment and David’s house.

outline.heading: Prayer for peace
outline.note: The psalm calls for prayer for Jerusalem’s peace and prosperity within its walls and palaces.

outline.heading: Seeking the city’s good
outline.note: The speaker seeks peace and good for Jerusalem because of companions and the house of Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: A Song of Ascents. By David. I was glad when they said to me, “Let’s go to Yahweh’s house!”
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the psalm its pilgrim joy and names Yahweh’s house as the destination.

keyVerses.text: where the tribes go up, even Yah’s tribes, according to an ordinance for Israel, to give thanks to Yahweh’s name.
keyVerses.why: This verse explains Jerusalem as a gathering point for Israel’s tribes and connects the journey with thanksgiving.

keyVerses.text: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem. Those who love you will prosper.
keyVerses.why: The psalm turns from description to direct prayer for Jerusalem’s peace.

keyVerses.text: For the sake of the house of Yahweh our God, I will seek your good.
keyVerses.why: The final verse grounds the speaker’s concern for the city in the house of Yahweh.

questions.question: What is a “Song of Ascents”?
questions.answer: The heading places this psalm among the Songs of Ascents, a group marked by the idea of going up. In this chapter that fits the movement toward Jerusalem and Yahweh’s house, especially when verse 4 says the tribes “go up.” The exact ancient performance setting is not described in the psalm, so it is better to notice the heading and movement without reconstructing every detail.

questions.question: Does “By David” prove David wrote this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading associates the psalm with David. Such headings are ancient, but their wording can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. Readers differ on which sense applies here; the heading establishes a Davidic association without settling every question about authorship.

questions.question: Why is the speaker glad to go to Yahweh’s house?
questions.answer: Verse 1 says the invitation itself makes the speaker glad. The rest of the psalm shows why the destination matters: Jerusalem is where the tribes give thanks, where judgment is associated with David’s house, and where the speaker seeks peace and good for the sake of Yahweh’s house.

questions.question: What does the psalm say about Jerusalem?
questions.answer: The psalm first places the speaker within Jerusalem’s gates. It then describes Jerusalem as compact together, a destination for the tribes, a place of thrones for judgment, and a city whose peace and prosperity are to be prayed for. The poem is not giving a full city history; it is presenting Jerusalem as the focus of worship, order, and shared concern.

questions.question: Who are “Yah’s tribes”?
questions.answer: Verse 4 identifies them as the tribes that go up to Jerusalem “according to an ordinance for Israel.” In the verse, their action is to give thanks to Yahweh’s name. The psalm does not list the tribes or explain the ordinance in detail.

questions.question: What are the “thrones for judgment”?
questions.answer: Verse 5 says thrones for judgment are set there and calls them “the thrones of David’s house.” The line links Jerusalem not only with worship but also with judgment or governance. The psalm does not describe a court case or specify who is sitting on the thrones in this moment.

questions.question: Does praying for Jerusalem’s peace mean the psalm ignores conflict or injustice?
questions.answer: The chapter asks for peace within Jerusalem’s walls and prosperity within its palaces, but it has just mentioned thrones for judgment. That combination suggests that peace is more than a private feeling; it belongs to the city’s public life as well. The psalm itself does not spell out a political program, so modern readers should keep some historical distance.

questions.question: Why does the speaker seek the city’s good for other people’s sake?
questions.answer: Verse 8 gives “my brothers’ and companions’ sakes” as the reason for saying, “Peace be within you.” The psalm’s love for Jerusalem is communal, not merely architectural. The speaker wants the city’s peace because other people’s lives are bound up with it.

questions.question: How does the final verse change the focus?
questions.answer: The last line says the speaker will seek Jerusalem’s good “for the sake of the house of Yahweh our God.” That returns the poem to the destination named in verse 1. The city matters in this psalm because it gathers people around Yahweh’s house.

glossary.def: The place named as the goal of the journey in verses 1 and 9; the psalm connects it with joy, prayer, and seeking Jerusalem’s good.
The city addressed in the psalm, described by its gates, compact form, tribes, thrones, walls, palaces, peace, and good.
The groups said to go up to Jerusalem to give thanks to Yahweh’s name.
The condition the psalm asks for within Jerusalem and speaks over the city for the sake of brothers and companions.
